results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
Every outline summary matches the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph, p01 to p55 in spec order; the three callouts match no spec paragraph.
The cold reverse outline lists the spec's controlling ideas in the spec's order across all eight sections, introduction and conclusion.
The outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas.
Each unit ties to S1-S6 through its section: the incident to S1/S3, definitions and the five parts to S2/S3, stored value to S4, choices and stages to S5, in-practice to S6, failures to S1/S3/S4.

Each table and figure is followed or introduced by a sentence saying what it shows: the incident table by the three faults, the type table by 'Read the last column', the allocation table by the refund paragraph, the options table by 'reading across a row', the stage table and the 2027 plan by the surrounding paragraphs; quotations from Adobe and Shopify are each tied to a claim.

Every boundary expresses its declared relationship and picks up the declared known information, e.g. contrast at 'Gift cards and loyalty points are not discounts', cause_effect at 'Three things went wrong', contrast at 'A refund gives back what was paid for goods', conclusion_summary at 'My rule', contrast at 'A written plan prevents the 2026 bug'.

results.quote: Her basket is the opening example's, but she uses no code (the worked allocation later tries one on it): her €199 jacket and two €18 pairs of socks total €235.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this sentence: three turns (same basket, no code, a later hypothetical code) arrive before the reader knows whether Eva is the opening shopper.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Black Friday Stacking Bug ¶3
results.quote: Noor Visser, who became Head of Engineering in January 2027, later put the incident next to the Price Drift of October 2026 (nine days in which the German storefront sold the Ridgewalker at €179 instead of €199 after a price-list sync failed silently)
results.finding: A second incident is brought in by a parenthesis at the end of the diagnosis and pays off only in the prior-price paragraph of In Practice; both readers called it a sideways jump.

results.quote: Shopify evaluates product discounts first, then order discounts on the reduced subtotal, then shipping discounts; that order took the Stacking Bug's jacket from €199 to €159.20 and then to €143.28.
results.finding: The incident ran on 'the shop platform', no vendor named; this sentence implies it is Shopify without saying so, and both readers stopped to check.

results.draft_locus: Gift Cards, Store Credit and Points: Ledgers, Not Promotions ¶2
results.quote: PwC's revenue guide on ASC 606 adds that breakage the merchant does not expect is recognized only when redemption becomes remote, and that unclaimed value that the law requires the merchant to hand to a government is a liability, not revenue.
results.finding: Both readers read the accounting paragraph twice; this sentence (expected vs unexpected breakage, 'remote', escheat) is where the density peaks.

results.draft_locus: Gift Cards, Store Credit and Points: Ledgers, Not Promotions ¶6
results.quote: Loyalty is split by the same separation of systems as the two gift-card pools: stores have a loyalty list; the online shop has no loyalty program. Noor and Milan deferred one until they could recognize the same customer across channels. Otherwise points could accumulate in an account the redemption system cannot identify. A shared balance service remains a goal after Waypoint
results.finding: Both readers re-read this paragraph: the opening comparison does not parse cleanly ('split' but one list and no program), 'Otherwise' attaches late, and Waypoint, the 2028 evaluation and W4 arrive in one sentence.

results.draft_locus: What a Promotion Is, and What It Touches ¶3
results.quote: In the EU it must obey the prior-price rule: an announced reduction must show the lowest price of the previous 30 days ("In Practice" gives the rule and its enforcement).
results.finding: Forward reference four sections ahead; one reader called it a small bump.

results.quote: The net price the fifth part writes to each line is then read outside the order.
results.finding: 'The fifth part' made one reader count back through the bolded parts; naming 'allocation' would save the look-back.

results.quote: Stop: Yes ... never with row 1 (the better one applies)
results.finding: One reader could not reconcile row 1's stop rule with 'the better one applies'; p42's evidence fixes these cell values as published (already an open question in the spec).

results.quote: The Stacking Bug's three costs had one cause: each time, a number was computed in one place and not recorded where the next system read it. The stacking rule was in a setting and not in the campaign plan
results.finding: One reader found the first example (a rule kept in a setting) does not fit 'a number computed and not recorded'; the wording is the spec's own synthesis and p50 controlling idea.

results.quote: the cart engine computes the final discount ... describes the five parts of a **promotion engine**
results.finding: 'Cart engine', 'promotion engine' and 'promotion system' are used for one thing and never said to be the same; minor.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Black Friday Stacking Bug ¶2
results.quote: The agency that customizes the storefront theme had enabled it for an October fleece campaign and left it on.
results.finding: 'Theme' is glossed only in The Choices ('the storefront's templates and front-end code'); minor.

results.quote: commercetools gives every cart discount a unique `sortOrder`
results.finding: commercetools is never said to be a commerce platform vendor; minor.

results.quote: It must be strongly consistent at redemption: two checkouts redeeming the last use of a single-use code in the same second must not both succeed.
results.finding: 'Strongly consistent' is not in already_knows and is never glossed as a term; only the example after the colon carries it.
results.corroborated_by: flow-A item 6 and flow-B item 5 also report 'strongly consistent' as not explained

results.quote: an absolute cart discount is distributed proportionately, evenly or individually across the lines.
results.finding: 'Absolute' (fixed-amount) and 'individually' are never explained; minor.

results.finding: Ravelin is not identified as a fraud-prevention vendor; minor.
Opens on a puzzling scenario (the returned jacket's refund), then bridges to stacking and stored value; none of the weak patterns.
The conclusion synthesizes, sorts claims by how settled they are and ends on questions and a hand-off; no new subtopic and no 'in conclusion'.
It states what no section states (the three costs and the gift-card mismatch share one cause) and the so-what: most incidents are prevented without new software by owning and writing these records.
'The chapter opened with a shopper who used a welcome code on a jacket and socks and returned the jacket. The refund is the jacket's net line price'.

Reader computes €179.10 from the proportional allocation (€19.90 to the jacket) and says the net price per line must be written to the order at order time, where returns, invoice and credit note read it.
Reader names the unowned, unchecked combination setting, then one owner, a written plan with order and stop rule, and a test against active promotions in staging, citing 'governance, not software'.
Reader says a gift card is prepaid value the merchant owes (a liability kept as a ledger) and that finance reconciles balances to the liability account monthly.

From the introduction alone the reader lists the sections in order (incident, definition, five parts and path to invoice/refund/books with Eva's allocation, stored value, four options by scale stage, dated examples and 2027 plan, failures) and the evidence: incident, worked allocation, three platforms' docs, accounting standards, a company filing.
